title: Who the customers were at each club
summary: Hoskins was mostly Black; the Elite somewhat mixed; the Panama loaded with whites from downtown and the West Side; Dago Frank's all white except pianist Bruce.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: I was going to ask you, all these places you have mentioned so far, the Panama, the De Luxe, and the Hot Shot and so forth, the people who came there, the customers --
Were they mostly black, or were they mixed, or what?
Well, when you got up to the -- when you got up to the Elite --
-- it was mixed. Not much. White fellows, a white person would come in in the Elite. But I don't remember the whites mixing down in Hoskin's, Hugh Hoskin's.

And the Panama. The Panama, yes, oh, yes. When they got to the Panama, the Panama was just loaded with white people. The colored people could hardly get in for the white people, because most of the people from downtown, the shows and things, aside from the show people.

Aside from the show people, people used to come from the West Side. That's where people with a lot of money used to come, the West Side. And well, like Hyde Park and those places, those people would come in.
So that Dago Frank's and Hoskin's, that was mostly black, or all black.
Well, Dago Frank's was nothing but white.
Dago Frank's was nothing but white.
Nothing but white, because Dago Frank's was down on the line, and that's where those sporting girls were, and nobody came in there but white people, white fellows.
Dago Frank's was 100 percent white. No colored. The only colored that was there was a fellow named Bruce who was a lousy piano player.
You know? That's the only colored fellow that was there.
